review.notes: Built on the course: buyer progress vs activity, exit criteria, qualification gates, stage probability from history, one source of truth, minimum fields, hygiene rules, coverage, win rate, stage conversion, cycle length, velocity, weighted pipeline, forecast categories. Calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Pioneer Supplies (fictional), a B2B distributor of office and cleaning supplies
content.briefing: Every month the sales forecast misses by 30%. Reps keep private lists, stages mean different things to different people, and deals sit untouched for months. You must build one pipeline and a forecast leadership can trust.

variants.text: A rep moved a deal to 'Offer submitted' because 'I sent the offer'. What is wrong with this as an exit criterion?

choices.t: It is seller activity, not buyer progress
choices.f: Better: 'the buyer agreed a date to review the offer'.
Sending says nothing about the buyer's commitment.
Checks help, but the criterion itself must be a buyer action.

variants.text: Which is a good exit criterion for 'Needs confirmed'?

choices.t: Buyer confirmed in writing; manager checks
choices.f: Buyer action, evidence and who checks it.

choices.t: The rep feels the needs are clear enough
choices.f: A feeling is not evidence.

choices.t: The rep held a meeting with the buyer
choices.f: A meeting is activity, not confirmation.

variants.text: Last year, 40 deals passed 'Terms agreed' and closed: 30 won, 10 lost. What probability do you use for that stage?

choices.f: Won from the stage / closed deals that passed it: 30 / 40.
Use your own history, not generic numbers.
That is the count won, not the rate.

variants.text: A rep wants to add a deal with no budget owner identified. Which gate does it fail?

choices.f: BANT or MEDDIC gates keep weak deals out.
Unqualified deals inflate the pipeline.
The issue is qualification, not value.

variants.text: Three reps keep private spreadsheets alongside the CRM.

choices.t: One shared pipeline for the whole team
choices.f: Forecasts and reviews use only the shared pipeline.

choices.t: Merge their lists by hand every month
choices.f: Slow and error-prone; the private lists remain.

choices.t: Let each rep pick their own tool
choices.f: No single view; the forecast stays unreliable.

variants.text: Which fields are minimum for every opportunity?

choices.t: Account, value basis, stage, date, next step
choices.f: Enough to review and forecast.

choices.t: Only the account name, to keep it light
choices.f: Too little to forecast.

choices.t: Fifty optional fields, to capture it all
choices.f: Too much; reps stop filling them.

variants.text: A deal's close date passed two weeks ago, and it is still open.

choices.t: Update the date or close it
choices.f: Hygiene rule: past close date means update or close.

choices.t: Leave it; it may still close
choices.f: Stale dates make the forecast wrong.

choices.t: Move it to next year quietly
choices.f: Moving dates without reason hides the problem.

variants.text: A deal has had no activity for 45 days. What does the hygiene rule say?

choices.t: Flag it as stale and review it
choices.f: No activity in 30 days means stale.
Untouched deals inflate the pipeline.
Inactivity lowers, not raises, the chance.

variants.text: Closed this year: 12 won, 28 lost, plus 15 still open. What is the win rate by count?

choices.f: Won / (won + lost) = 12 / 40. Exclude open deals.
You included open deals: 12 / 55.
That is won / lost, not won / closed.

variants.text: Win rate is 30%. Roughly what pipeline coverage do you need?

choices.f: Required coverage is about 1 / win rate.
Only if you won every deal.
That confuses the percentage.

variants.text: Open pipeline for the quarter: Kz 90 m. Remaining target: Kz 30 m. What is coverage?

choices.f: 90 / 30. Compare it with the coverage you need.
You divided the wrong way.
That is the difference, not coverage.

variants.text: 100 deals entered 'Qualified'; 40 reached 'Needs confirmed'. What is the stage conversion?

choices.f: Reached next / entered stage. It shows where deals stall.
That is the share that did not move on.
Divided the wrong way.

variants.text: To measure the average sales cycle, which deals do you use?

choices.f: Average days from created to won.
Open deals have no end date.
Lost deals do not show how long winning takes.

variants.text: 40 opportunities, 25% win rate, average deal Kz 2 m, cycle 50 days. Sales velocity?

choices.f: You forgot to divide by the cycle length.
You left out the win rate.

variants.text: Deals: Kz 10 m at 25%, Kz 20 m at 50%, Kz 8 m at 75%. Weighted pipeline?

choices.f: That is the unweighted total.
You applied the average probability (50%) to the total. Weight each deal separately.

variants.text: A deal has a signed contract waiting only for the PO number. Which category?

choices.f: High confidence, evidence-based.
Best case is possible but less certain.
It is far beyond early stage.

variants.text: Leadership wants one forecast number. What do you give?

choices.t: Closed + commit, with best case as upside
choices.f: Categories show certainty levels honestly.
That assumes every deal wins.
A target is not a forecast.

variants.text: The weighted pipeline looks good, but the CEO doubts it. Why can weighted forecasts mislead?

choices.t: Weak with few big deals or poor stage data
choices.f: One big deal swings it; check with categories and deal review.

choices.t: They are always too low by design
choices.f: They can be high or low.

choices.t: Weights are never useful for forecasting
choices.f: Useful, but not alone.

variants.text: When does the weekly exception report run?

choices.f: Daily updates, weekly exceptions before review, monthly clean-up.
Problems pile up for three months.
Too late to fix anything.

variants.text: Every lost deal must have:

choices.f: Lost reasons show what to fix in products, price or process.
You lose the lesson.
Deleting data hides the history.
